title: Κύων ⟨θηρευτικὸς καὶ κύνες⟩
titleEn: The Hunting Dog and the Dogs
part: The Hunting Dog and the Dogs (Chambry 179 · Perry 329)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 179 (= Perry 329). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κύων τρεφόμενος ἐν οἴκῳ, θηρσὶν εἰδὼς μάχεσθαι, ἰδὼν πολλοὺς ἐν τάξει ἱσταμένους, ῥήξας τὸν κλοιὸν τοῦ τραχήλου, ἔφευγε διὰ τῶν ἀμφόδων.
sentences.tr: Kyōn trephomenos en oikōi, thērsin eidōs machesthai, idōn pollous en taxei histamenous, rhēxas ton kloion tou trachēlou, epheuge dia tōn amphodōn.
sentences.l: A dog being kept in a house, knowing how to fight with wild beasts, seeing many standing drawn up in rank, having broken the collar from his neck, was fleeing through the streets.
sentences.i: A dog kept in the house, knowing how to fight wild beasts, saw many of them drawn up in line, broke the collar from his neck, and fled off through the streets.
sentences.n: A chain of participles (τρεφόμενος, εἰδώς, ἰδών, ῥήξας) hangs on the one finite verb ἔφευγε — the ordinary engine of these fables. μάχομαι takes the dative of the one fought, θηρσίν. What the dog sees is left unnamed: πολλούς is simply "many", and ἐν τάξει ἱσταμένους is "standing in formation"; the beasts he is set against are the likeliest thing being drawn up, but the Greek does not say so. τὰ ἄμφοδα are the blocks of a town, and so the streets that run between them.

sentences.t: Κύνες δὲ ἄλλοι τοῦτον ἰδόντες εὐτραφῆ οἷα ταῦρον εἶπον· « Τί φεύγεις ; »
sentences.tr: Kynes de alloi touton idontes eutraphē hoia tauron eipon· « Ti pheugeis ; »
sentences.l: But other dogs, seeing him well-fed like a bull, said: « Why are you running away? »
sentences.n: οἷα with the accusative makes a loose comparison, "such as, like". εὐτραφής is "well-nourished" — the plenty the dog goes on to weigh against what it costs him.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν· « Ὅτι μὲν τροφῇ συζῶ περισσῇ οἶδα καὶ σῶμα τὸ ἐμὸν εὐφραίνω· ἀεὶ δὲ πλησίον εἰμὶ θανάτου, ἄρκοις καὶ λέουσι μαχόμενος. »
sentences.tr: Ho de eipen· « Hoti men trophēi syzō perissēi oida kai sōma to emon euphrainō· aei de plēsion eimi thanatou, arkois kai leousi machomenos. »
sentences.l: And he said: « That I live amid food to spare I know, and I make my own body glad; but I am always near death, fighting with bears and lions. »
sentences.i: And he said: « I know that I live with food to spare and keep my own body content; but I am always close to death, fighting bears and lions. »
sentences.n: Here ὅτι is a subordinator with its governing verb expressed, οἶδα, which the clause stands in front of: quite unlike the bare Ὅτι that opens the moral below. περισσῇ agrees with τροφῇ across the intervening verb. μέν … δέ sets the plenty against the danger it is bought with.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ πρὸς ἀλλήλους εἶπον· « Καλὸν βίον ἡμεῖς, εἰ καὶ πενιχρόν, ζῶμεν, οἵτινες οὔτε λέουσι οὔτε ἄρκοις μαχόμεθα. »
sentences.tr: Hoi de pros allēlous eipon· « Kalon bion hēmeis, ei kai penichron, zōmen, hoitines oute leousi oute arkois machometha. »
sentences.l: And they said to one another: « A fine life we live, even if a poor one, we who fight neither lions nor bears. »
sentences.n: βίον is a cognate accusative with ζῶμεν, "we live a life". εἰ καί concedes the point, "even if". οἵτινες is the causal relative: not merely "who" but "seeing that we".

sentences.t: Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ κινδύνους ἑαυτῷ ἐπιφέρειν διὰ τρυφὴν καὶ ματαίαν δόξαν, ἀλλὰ τούτους ἐκφεύγειν.
sentences.tr: Hoti ou dei kindynous heautōi epipherein dia tryphēn kai mataian doxan, alla toutous ekpheugein.
sentences.l: That one must not bring dangers upon oneself for the sake of luxury and empty repute, but flee them.
sentences.i: The story shows that one must not bring dangers upon oneself for the sake of luxury and empty repute, but must flee them.
sentences.n: The introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek — Ὅτι stands as though "the story shows" had come before it — and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἐπιφέρω with the dative is to bring a thing upon someone, here upon oneself. δόξα is the opinion others hold of a man, and ματαία δόξα is repute with nothing behind it.
